author: kallupx
body:
## Description

Add native rendered previews for local Markdown and a bounded HTML subset. Documents can be switched between **Rendered** and **Source**, while **Render documents by default** controls the initial view of newly opened documents without persisting per-file choices.

Markdown is parsed with `pulldown-cmark`, while HTML is tokenized with `html5gum` and rendered using native GTK widgets. Supported content includes headings, paragraphs, formatting, nested lists, quotes, HTTP(S) links, code blocks, rules, and tables. Code blocks support theme-aware syntax highlighting and one-click copying.

Large rendered and source previews use recycled, virtualized rows so navigation, selection, and memory remain bounded. Cross-row selection, Ctrl+C, table copying, code copying, live theme changes, cancellation, and stale-request rejection are supported.

The HTML renderer does not use WebKit or Chromium, execute JavaScript, apply CSS, load subresources, or provide parser-initiated filesystem or network access. Unsafe and active content remains inert or is omitted with a visible warning.

## Visual evidence


https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/606f81b9-701f-4ef0-8f25-862719ea9f75


## How to test

1. Open local Markdown and HTML files containing headings, formatted text, nested lists, quotes, code blocks, links, rules, and tables.
2. Toggle between **Rendered** and **Source** using the preview action.
3. Change **Settings → General → Browsing → Render documents by default**, then open another document.
4. Drag across headings, paragraphs, lists, code blocks, and tables; press `Ctrl+C` and verify the copied text.
5. Use the copy button on highlighted and plain code blocks.
6. Activate HTTP(S) links and confirm unsupported schemes remain inert.
7. Browse large fixtures rapidly and scroll through their rendered and source views.
8. Open malformed, unsupported, oversized, deeply nested, and active-content fixtures.

**Expected result:** Supported local documents render with native, theme-aware styling. Selection and copying work across the preview, large files remain responsive, unsafe content stays inert, and unavailable rendering falls back to Source with a clear explanation.

## Verification

- [x] Static review of parser, renderer, GTK ownership, worker lifecycle, cancellation, links, gestures, and lazy view creation.
- [x] Security probes for NUL bytes, malformed markup, escaping, unsafe URI schemes, nested links, and unintended link activation.
- [x] Adversarial approximately 1 MiB documents exercising event, depth, markup, table, time, and cancellation limits.
- [x] Performance measurements in debug and release builds.
- [x] Memory profiling with span-heavy documents and repeated GTK row materialization.
- [x] Leak and lifecycle tests using weak GTK references and `G_DEBUG=fatal-criticals`.
- [x] Interaction checks covering clicking, dragging, cross-row selection, copying, and drag thresholds.
- [x] Regression tests for nested and repeated styles, list and table boundaries, worker panics, and pre-token cancellation.
- [x] Every review round ran formatting, Clippy with warnings denied, and the complete test suite, ending at 313 passing tests before the final rebase.
- [x] Final rebased `./scripts/check.sh`: 413 tests passed.
- [x] Final optimized release build completed successfully.

Adds `html5gum 0.8.4` with default features disabled. The optimized binary grows by approximately 0.73 MiB, or 5.9%.

## Related issue

Closes #89

issues.body:
### Problem or use case

Strata's one-click/Space quick preview currently shows Markdown and HTML files as source text. Users should be able to read these documents in a styled, rendered view without opening another application.

HTML introduces a design and security constraint: Strata must not bundle Chromium or quietly turn the preview pane into a general-purpose browser. We need a bounded approach that is useful for ordinary static documents while preserving the existing preview trust boundary and package footprint.

### Proposed solution

Add first-class rendered document content to the existing quick-preview drawer for local Markdown and HTML files.

#### Markdown

- Detect common Markdown extensions and MIME types (`.md`, `.markdown`, and equivalents).
- Parse Markdown with the existing `pulldown-cmark` dependency, extracting/reusing the safe release-note rendering work where practical.
- Render headings, paragraphs, emphasis, lists, block quotes, links, inline code, fenced code blocks, horizontal rules, and task lists as native GTK widgets/text with readable spacing and typography.
- Apply Strata's semantic theme tokens to every element and update live when the theme changes.

#### HTML

Begin with a short feasibility/design spike, then implement the smallest safe static-document renderer that meets the constraints below:

- Do **not** add or bundle Chromium/Electron, launch a hidden external browser, or create a general browser surface.
- Prefer parsing HTML and mapping a documented semantic subset to the same native GTK rich-document model used by Markdown (headings, paragraphs, lists, block quotes, links, pre/code, tables, and basic text emphasis).
- Compare that approach with a system WebKitGTK dependency only if native rendering cannot provide a useful result; document package-size, runtime, sandbox, and security implications before selecting it. A browser engine must not be added merely for pixel-perfect page rendering.
- Treat scripts, styles that can fetch resources, forms, frames, embedded objects, event handlers, and active content as unsupported/inert.
- Never execute JavaScript or automatically load remote resources, local sibling files, fonts, images, media, or other subresources.
- If browser-faithful HTML cannot be supported within these constraints, clearly define the supported static subset and fall back to source text for unsupported documents rather than adding Chromium.

#### Shared preview behavior

- Use the existing one-click/Space preview drawer, cancellation/request identity, metadata header, open-in-default-app action, and 1 MiB text read cap.
- Keep parsing/render-model construction off GTK's main thread for non-trivial documents and make stale results harmless.
- Provide a toggle between **Rendered** and **Source** for Markdown and HTML, remembering the choice only if that fits the existing preference model.
- Keep links inert until clicked; open allowed `http`/`https` links through the normal external URI handler. Do not activate unsafe URI schemes.
- Show a clear bounded fallback for malformed, oversized, unsupported, or failed documents.
- Keep remote-file previews out of scope unless a separately defined bounded download policy exists.

### Alternatives considered

- Continue showing source text only. This is safe and simple but not useful for reading formatted documents.
- Bundle Chromium/Electron. Rejected because of dependency size, maintenance burden, and browser attack surface.
- Render every HTML page exactly like a browser. This requires a full web engine and conflicts with the intended lightweight, safe preview model.
- Open the default browser automatically. This is not an inline preview and would make one-click browsing disruptive.
- Convert HTML/Markdown by shelling out to external tools. This creates inconsistent availability and complicates sandboxing and failure handling.

### Visual examples

N/A — reuse the existing quick-preview drawer. The implementation PR should include before/after screenshots for representative Markdown and static HTML files.

### Strata version

0.5.0

### Additional context

#### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Selecting a supported Markdown file renders a styled document in the existing quick-preview drawer.
- [ ] Selecting a supported static HTML file renders the documented safe subset, or falls back clearly when the document requires unsupported browser features.
- [ ] Markdown and HTML previews offer a source view without changing the file.
- [ ] No Chromium/Electron runtime is added or bundled.
- [ ] HTML scripts, event handlers, forms, frames, embedded objects, and active content never execute.
- [ ] Previewing a document causes no automatic network requests or subresource/file loading.
- [ ] Unsafe link schemes are inert; allowed web links require an explicit click and open externally.
- [ ] Reads, parser work, output/widget count, nesting depth, and rendering time are bounded so adversarial documents cannot freeze or exhaust the UI.
- [ ] Malformed, oversized, timed-out, cancelled, or unsupported documents degrade to source text or the normal unavailable state without crashing Strata.
- [ ] All visual states use semantic theme colors, update live, remain keyboard accessible, and expose appropriate accessible roles/names.
- [ ] Tests cover content classification, Markdown constructs, the supported HTML subset, sanitization/active-content rejection, resource-loading prohibition, malformed/deep documents, limits, cancellation/stale results, source toggling, and live theme behavior.
- [ ] Documentation states the supported Markdown/HTML features and the chosen HTML rendering architecture/security boundary.

body: ## Description Detect pacman ownership of the running Strata executable and keep package-managed copies on the system update path. Omarchy and Arch users still receive release notices and notes, but the update surfaces open Omarchy’s interactive updater in the configured terminal, and the installer rejects package-owned targets before downloading. Manual release binaries retain in-place updates. Document `omarchy pkg add strata` as the Omarchy installation path and `omarchy update` as its update path. ## Visual evidence ## How to test 1. Install Strata on Omarchy with `omarchy pkg add strata`, launch it, and open **Settings → Updates**. 2. Check against a newer release and open the sidebar release notice. 3. Repeat with a release archive installed under `~/.local/bin`. **Expected result:** The OPR copy says it is managed by Omarchy, opens `omarchy update` in the configured terminal, and never offers an in-app download. The per-user archive copy still offers the in-app installer. ## Related issue Closes #195

issues.body:
## Problem or use case

Strata is now distributed through the Omarchy Package Repository as `omarchy/strata`. The in-app updater currently stages and replaces the running executable directly. For an OPR installation, `/usr/bin/strata` is owned by pacman: replacement normally fails due to permissions and would desynchronize pacman’s package database if Strata were run with enough privilege.

The installation documentation also still says Strata only publishes release archives and directs all Omarchy users through a manual archive installation.

## Proposed solution

- Detect when the running executable is owned by a system package.
- Continue allowing release checks and release notes, but do not offer or run in-place installation for package-managed copies.
- Clearly direct package-managed users to their system updater. For Omarchy/Arch, avoid partial-upgrade advice.
- Keep in-place updates available for user-installed release binaries such as `~/.local/bin/strata`.
- Update the README so Omarchy users install Strata with `omarchy pkg add strata`; retain archive instructions for other supported environments.
- Add tests for package ownership classification and update UI behavior.

## Alternatives considered

- Treat every executable under `/usr/bin` as package managed. This is only a heuristic and can misclassify manually installed files.
- Let replacement fail on filesystem permissions. This gives users a late, confusing error and does not enforce package-manager ownership as an updater invariant.
- Disable update checks entirely. Checks and release notes remain useful; only installation needs to defer to the package manager.

## Visual examples

The Settings → Updates action should identify that Strata is managed by the system instead of displaying “Install update.”

## Strata version

0.8.0

## Additional context

Ryan Hughes announced `omarchy/strata 0.8.0-1` in OPR. This is related to, but distinct from, the AUR packaging work in #50 / #183.

author: pdwaldrop
body:
## Description

Update checking hit the GitHub API unconditionally on every launch and every Settings → Updates visit: `load_current_release_notes` refetched the *installed* version's notes every time despite that release being immutable, and the latest-release probe had no cache and no minimum interval between checks. Users behind CGNAT, a corporate NAT, or a shared VPN exit could exhaust the unauthenticated 60 req/hr limit.

This implements the caching approach proposed in the issue:

- The installed version's release notes are now cached permanently under `~/.cache/strata/release-notes.toml`, keyed by tag, so a given release's notes are fetched at most once, ever.
- The latest-release probe is cached under `~/.cache/strata/update-check.toml` with a 6-hour floor (persisted across restarts) on automatic checks. `check_for_updates` gained a `force: bool` — only the explicit "Check now" button and a channel switch pass `true`; startup and re-enabling "Automatically check for updates" pass `false` and respect the floor/cache.
- Requests send `If-None-Match` when an ETag is cached, and a `304` is treated as "unchanged" (reusing the cached release list without re-parsing).

**Caveat found during manual testing, disclosed rather than hidden:** the `If-None-Match` handling is implemented correctly, but testing directly against the live API (both `/releases/latest` and the list endpoint) shows GitHub returns `200` rather than `304` for unauthenticated requests, even with a confirmed-matching, confirmed-stable ETag. The code is harmless and matches the issue's request, but in practice it's the 6-hour floor and the permanent notes cache doing the actual work of reducing traffic, not the conditional-request path.

Out of scope, per the issue's own "Additional context": `perform_install`'s use of `fs::rename` to replace the running executable is not safe against a pacman-owned path once an AUR package exists — tracked separately once packaging is decided, not part of this change.

## Visual evidence

N/A — this changes update-check request/caching plumbing with no user-visible UI difference beyond fewer rate-limit errors under heavy launch/restart frequency.

## How to test

1. Build and run Strata, then open Settings → Updates (or just let it start with "Automatically check for updates" enabled).
2. Check `~/.cache/strata/release-notes.toml` and `~/.cache/strata/update-check.toml` exist with sensible content (tag/notes; channel/checked_at/etag/releases respectively).
3. Quit and relaunch within 6 hours — `update-check.toml`'s `checked_at` and file mtime should be unchanged, confirming no redundant network request.
4. Click "Check now" in Settings → Updates — this should always force a fresh request regardless of the floor.
5. Switch the release channel (Stable/Preview/Nightly) — should force a fresh check for the new channel rather than reusing the previous channel's cache.

**Expected result:** at most one automatic latest-release request per channel per 6 hours, and the installed version's release notes are fetched only once per version, across restarts.

## Related issue

Closes #181

issues.body:
### Problem or use case

Update checking goes through the GitHub REST API (`https://api.github.com/repos/lgse/strata/releases`, `src/services/update_check.rs:11`), which allows 60 unauthenticated requests per hour per source IP. Users behind CGNAT, a corporate NAT, or a shared VPN exit can exhaust that and see "GitHub API rate limit reached".

The app also spends that quota more than it needs to:

- `src/ui/settings.rs:585` re-fetches the **installed** version's release notes on every open of Settings → Updates. That release is immutable, so every fetch after the first is wasted.
- `src/ui/settings.rs:689` and the startup auto-check hit `/releases/latest` with no cache and no minimum interval between checks.
- No request sends `If-None-Match`, so no repeat can come back as a free `304`.

For reference, Omarchy avoids the GitHub API entirely: `omarchy-update-available` runs `checkupdates` against its own pacman repo, and the bar widget polls it on a 6-hour timer (`shell/plugins/bar/widgets/SystemUpdate.qml`).

### Proposed solution

Cache aggressively and rate-limit ourselves, rather than changing where the data comes from:

- Cache the installed version's release notes permanently under `~/.cache/strata/`, keyed by version, so `load_current_release_notes` fetches at most once per version.
- Put a 6-hour floor on the latest-version probe (matching Omarchy's interval), persisted so a restart does not re-check.
- Send `If-None-Match` and treat `304` as "unchanged"; conditional requests do not count against the GitHub rate limit.

Together these remove nearly all recurring API traffic while keeping the existing endpoints and `parse_markdown` untouched.

### Alternatives considered

- **A `latest.json` manifest** published by `.github/workflows/release.yml` to `raw.githubusercontent.com` or GitHub Pages, both CDN-served and outside the API rate limit. Would also carry per-arch asset URLs and metadata the API has no equivalent for (minimum supported version, yank flag, glibc floor). Heavier than the caching work and worth revisiting only if rate-limit reports continue after it.
- **`https://github.com/lgse/strata/releases.atom`** — the version and notes in one non-API request, but notes arrive as HTML rather than the Markdown `parse_markdown` expects.
- **`/releases/latest` with redirects disabled** — version only from the `Location` header, no notes or assets.
- **Authenticating the API requests** — raises the limit to 5000/hr but requires shipping a token in a client binary. Rejected.

### Visual examples

N/A — the change is to update-check plumbing, with no user-visible difference beyond fewer rate-limit errors.

### Strata version

0.7.0

### Additional context

## Description

List thumbnails for camera RAW files now try the embedded JPEG/PPM extract before pixbuf or ImageMagick. ImageMagick typically demosaics, so when it ran first the cheap camera preview never ran. Full-size `preview-image` still uses pixbuf → ImageMagick → dcraw.

## Visual evidence

```
strata perf/198-raw-thumbnail-preview  ? ❯ STRATA_RAW_BENCH="/run/media/oscar/wd_black/Photos RAW/Grand Canyon" cargo test --release -- --ignored --nocapture bench_raw_thumbnail
    Finished `release` profile [optimized] target(s) in 0.07s
     Running unittests src/main.rs (target/release/deps/strata-1e6c0000011fc478)

running 1 test
141 RAW files under /run/media/oscar/wd_black/Photos RAW/Grand Canyon
test sandbox_helper::tests::bench_raw_thumbnail has been running for over 60 seconds
thumbnail-order (dcraw → pixbuf → ImageMagick): 141 ok  0 fail  total 2.3s  median 16.3ms
preview-order    (pixbuf → ImageMagick → dcraw): 141 ok  0 fail  total 83.9s  median 549.8ms
test sandbox_helper::tests::bench_raw_thumbnail ... ok

test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 376 filtered out; finished in 86.21s
```
I compared the two orders and the results are quite good, from a median of 550 to 16.3 milliseconds.

## How to test

1. Open a directory of camera RAW files (for example `.ARW`) in Grid or any view that shows list thumbnails.
2. Confirm tiles appear and look like the camera’s embedded preview (same as a machine without ImageMagick).
3. Open one of those files in the preview pane.

**Expected result:** Thumbnails resolve from the embedded extract when `dcraw`/`simple_dcraw` can provide one, without waiting on a full demosaic. The preview pane still uses the existing demosaic-first RAW path.

issues.body:
**Problem or use case**


Browsing a directory with many camera RAW files is slow to fill thumbnails, especially when ImageMagick is installed.

thumbnail-raw and preview-image currently share render_raw in src/sandbox_helper.rs:

  gdk pixbuf → magick/convert -auto-orient -thumbnail → dcraw -e -c → simple_dcraw -e

dcraw -e / simple_dcraw -e extract the embedded JPEG/PPM preview. ImageMagick typically demosaics the RAW. If ImageMagick succeeds, the cheap extract never runs.

Hosts without ImageMagick already get embedded-preview thumbnails. Hosts with ImageMagick get a slower, different-looking thumbnail. 

_**Note**: List/preview SIZE, MODIFIED, and TYPE are GIO/FileEntry fields and are not produced by this helper; this issue is thumbnail pixels only._


**Proposed solution**


Give thumbnail-raw its own chain so embedded extract runs first. Leave preview-image on the current chain so the 1400px pane can still demosaic when ImageMagick works.

  thumbnail-raw:  dcraw -e / simple_dcraw -e → pixbuf → magick/convert
  preview-image:  pixbuf → magick/convert → dcraw -e / simple_dcraw -e  (unchanged)

Reuse the existing render_dcraw, render_pixbuf, and render_imagemagick helpers. Keep sandbox/bwrap, fallbacks, orientation on the embedded path (same as hosts that already lacked ImageMagick), and JPEG/PNG/WebP/TIFF thumbnail-image unchanged.


**Alternatives considered**


- Reorder preview-image as well: faster RAW pane, but 1400px appearance can change from demosaic to embedded JPEG. Out of scope.
- JPEG EXIF thumbnails for ordinary images: often ~160×120; doubtful win vs from_file_at_scale. Out of scope.
- Raising MAX_THUMBNAIL_WORKERS: separate issue.
- Caching thumbs after unbind: possible separate issue/PR.
- New image libraries or bypassing the sandbox: rejected.


**Visual examples:** 

N/A — helper fallback order, not a visual redesign.

**Version:**

source build (main)

**Additional context**


Files: src/sandbox_helper.rs, src/sandbox_helper/tests.rs. Update docs/preview-sandbox.md only if it would otherwise be wrong about thumbnail RAW order.

Do not change src/ui/thumbnail.rs, FileEntry, GIO query_info, preview UI, or MAX_THUMBNAIL_WORKERS.

Helper result.meta is PDF page numbers only; thumbnail-raw and preview-image pass None. This change does not affect metadata speed or contents.

author: JoeJoeflyn
body:
## Summary

- Store `is_hidden` on `FileEntry` at enumeration time
- Keep all entries in memory; filter hidden files at the UI level via `CustomFilter`
- `toggle_hidden` flips a boolean and calls `filter.changed()` — no disk re-enumeration, no monitor reinstallation
- Extracted shared `entry_filter()` helper to avoid duplicated filter closures across columns, grid, and explorer panes

## Why

Toggling hidden files re-enumerated every open column from disk AND tore down + reinstalled every directory monitor, all sequential on the main thread. For 5 open columns that's 5 disk reads + 5 monitor recreations — the freeze users see.

The fix keeps all entries (including hidden ones) in memory and lets GTK's virtualized `FilterListModel` hide/show them instantly. The `is_hidden` flag is encoded in the model value (`"dh\t.config"` vs `"dv\tREADME.md"`) so the filter closure can check it in O(1) without a side lookup.

Memory cost: ~132 bytes per hidden entry, bounded by the existing 100k `MAX_DIRECTORY_ENTRIES` cap. Negligible — a single thumbnail uses more RAM.

## Manual verification

1. Open a directory with several columns
2. Toggle "Show Hidden Files" on and off repeatedly
3. Toggle is instant with no freeze

## Expected result

Hidden files appear/disappear instantly on toggle with no UI freeze.

Closes #200

## Description

Pinned folders could only be arranged by unpinning and re-pinning them. They are now reorderable by drag and drop, using the same interaction, cursor, and drop styling as the standard folders (Desktop, Documents, Downloads, …).

Reordering stays inside the Pinned section: the drag payload is namespaced with a `pinned:` prefix, so a standard row rejects a pinned payload and a pinned row rejects a standard one. Rows carry their index into the stored bookmark list, so bookmarks hidden from the Pinned section (those that resolve to standard folders) keep their place in the file. The new order is written back to the GTK bookmarks file, so it is restored on the next launch.

## Visual evidence

N/A — no new elements or styling. The rows reuse the existing `.sidebar-row.reorderable` drag/drop appearance, so before/after screenshots are identical outside of the drag itself.

## How to test

1. Pin at least three folders (right-click a folder in the file list → Pin).
2. Drag a pinned row above and below other pinned rows; drop on the upper half of a row to place it before, the lower half to place it after.
3. Try dragging a pinned row onto a standard folder row, and a standard folder row onto a pinned row.
4. Restart Strata.

**Expected result:** Pinned rows reorder to the drop position and the Pinned section keeps its own order; cross-section drags do nothing; the order from step 2 is still in place after the restart.

## Related issue

Closes #184

author: spandan11106
body:
## Description

Marquee selection had to begin on empty space inside a file pane. A directory long
enough to fill and scroll the viewport leaves no such space, so mouse-only
multi-selection was impractical in Explorer.

The two near-identical marquee implementations (columns view in `ui::browser`,
grid/explorer panes in `ui::browser_modes`) now live in a shared `ui::marquee`
module, which also supports starting a drag on inert chrome outside a pane and
carrying it into the pane:

- **Sidebar** — blank panel space, in every mode. This is the most reachable
  origin, since the sidebar sits beside all three views. It targets the pane
  nearest the start edge: the explorer or grid pane, or the first open column.
- **Explorer** — the pane header and the column-heading strip.
- **Grid** — the pane header.
- **Columns** — each column header, plus the blank strip beside the last open
  column; a drag there targets the last column.

A press landing on a button, entry, slider, or scrollbar is left to that control,
so navigation, sorting, column resizing, scrollbars, and the sidebar's own place
rows (which are buttons) keep their existing behaviour. GTK keeps the event
sequence on the originating widget once the gesture is claimed, so the drag
continues into the file list without further routing.

Two supporting changes make cross-pane drags behave:

- The anchor is stored in the view's own coordinates and the pointer in the
  scrolled window's, so the band stays glued to the content while the list moves.
- Holding the pointer near a viewport edge auto-scrolls the list, with the band
  and selection recomputed each frame. Axes the view cannot scroll contribute
  nothing, so the timer does not spin against a fixed edge.

The band is also clipped to its overlay instead of only being clamped at the
origin, so a drag beginning above or beside the view no longer paints outside it.

### Explorer now activates on double click

Please review this part specifically — it is a deliberate behaviour change.

Explorer set `single_click_activate(true)`. GTK bundles two behaviours into that
property: "activate rows on single click **and select them on hover**". The hover
half replaced the whole selection with whatever row the pointer crossed, which
discarded a marquee the instant the drag ended.

This was not caused by this branch and was not limited to the marquee — on `main`,
hover-select already made Ctrl+Click and Shift+Click multi-selection unusable in
Explorer, since moving the pointer collapsed the selection to one row. GTK offers
no way to keep single-click activation without hover selection, so Explorer now
activates on a double click, matching the grid and column views which already do.

## Visual evidence

N/A — the change is an interaction rather than a new visual element, and I have no
screen capture tooling on this machine. Happy to add a recording before merge.

## How to test

1. Open a directory with enough entries to fill and scroll the viewport, in Explorer.
2. Press blank sidebar space (the area below the last place) and drag right into the
   rows. Repeat from the pane header and from the column-heading strip.
3. Keep dragging past the bottom edge of the list.
4. Repeat step 2 in Grid, and in List from the blank strip right of the last column.
5. Ctrl+Click and Shift+Click several rows in Explorer, then move the pointer across
   the list.
6. Confirm the untouched paths: click a heading to sort, drag a column resize handle,
   drag the scrollbar, drag a row to move a file, click a sidebar place to navigate,
   drag a sidebar place to reorder it, and double-click a folder in Explorer to open it.

**Expected result:** a rubber band appears from the press point and selects every row
it crosses; step 3 scrolls the list and keeps extending the selection; the step 5
selection survives pointer movement; everything in step 6 behaves as before, except
that Explorer now opens on a double click.

## Related issue

Closes #189

issues.body:
### Problem or use case

Marquee selection currently has to begin on empty space inside a file pane. In List/Explorer mode, a directory with enough rows to fill and scroll the viewport leaves little or no empty space, making mouse-based selection of multiple files impractical without modifier-clicking or using the keyboard.

### Proposed solution

Explore whether a marquee drag can begin in adjacent empty space outside a file pane and continue into the pane to select files.

The implementation should determine:

- which surrounding regions can safely initiate selection without conflicting with navigation, column resizing, scrollbars, or other controls;
- whether GTK gesture capture can maintain the drag as it crosses into the file list;
- how coordinates and hit testing should be translated into the target pane;
- whether dragging near the pane edges should auto-scroll through a long list; and
- whether the behavior can work consistently across List/Explorer, Grid, and Columns modes.

At minimum, users should have a practical mouse-only way to begin marquee selection when rows fill the entire List/Explorer viewport. Existing Ctrl+Click, Shift+Click, keyboard selection, row dragging, and empty-space marquee behavior must continue to work.

### Alternatives considered

- Require a modifier while beginning a drag on a row. This can work technically but is less discoverable and still conflicts with dragging files.
- Rely on Ctrl+Click, Shift+Click, or keyboard range selection. These remain useful but do not replace direct marquee selection.
- Add permanent blank space inside the viewport. This wastes limited space and does not help users begin selection near a specific visible range.

### Visual examples

N/A — include a short recording of selection beginning outside a full, scrollable list if the interaction proves feasible.

### Strata version

Current development build.

### Additional context

This is partly an interaction and GTK event-routing exploration. If cross-pane marquee initiation is not reliable, document the constraint and implement the closest practical mouse-first alternative.

author: pdwaldrop
body:
## Description

Moving a non-empty directory to a different filesystem (e.g. a Btrfs home directory to a tmpfs `/tmp`) failed outright with "Can't recursively copy directory," leaving the source intact and the destination empty. `g_file_move` renames when it can, but for a directory it never silently recurses to cross a filesystem boundary — it returns `G_IO_ERROR_WOULD_RECURSE` instead of doing a partial, unsafe copy, and the transfer/restore code just propagated that as a hard failure.

This adds `move_local`/`move_local_with`: it attempts the normal move first (a same-filesystem move stays a cheap rename), and on `WouldRecurse` specifically falls back to the existing `copy_new_recursively` — the same staged-copy-then-atomic-rename machinery already used for safe directory copies and replacements elsewhere in this file — deleting the source only once that copy has fully and durably succeeded. Cancellation or any other failure leaves the source untouched, since the fallback reuses `copy_new_recursively`'s own staging cleanup rather than new logic.

Applied at both call sites that perform a plain move: the paste/cut flow (the reported case) and trash restore, which has the identical `move_async`-with-no-fallback pattern and would hit the same failure restoring a trashed directory to a different filesystem.

## Visual evidence

N/A — this is a backend transfer-logic fix. Before, the operation failed with an error dialog; after, it succeeds silently like any other move. There's no new or changed UI to show.

## How to test

1. Create a non-empty directory on one filesystem (e.g. your Btrfs/ext4 home directory): `mkdir -p ~/xdev-source/nested && echo top > ~/xdev-source/top.txt && echo child > ~/xdev-source/nested/child.txt`.
2. In Strata, cut (`Ctrl+X`) that directory and paste (`Ctrl+V`) it into a location on a different filesystem, such as `/tmp` (typically tmpfs).
3. Also test trash restore: trash a directory, then restore it to a location on a different filesystem than the trash's own (if applicable to your setup).

**Expected result:** the move completes successfully — the destination contains the full directory contents, and the source is gone. No "Can't recursively copy directory" error.

I verified this directly against a real Btrfs-to-tmpfs move in addition to the new unit tests (which inject `WouldRecurse` and other failures instead of requiring an actual second filesystem, keeping them portable across environments): source correctly removed, destination created with byte-correct nested content.

## Related issue

Closes #150

issues.body:
### Strata version
Source build at commit `e9f6dd0` (0.6.1).

### Installation method

### Linux distribution and desktop environment

### What happened?
Moving a directory between filesystems fails immediately. Strata displays “Unable to complete operation” with the detail “Can’t recursively copy directory.” The source remains intact and the destination remains empty.

### Steps to reproduce
1. Create a non-empty directory on a Btrfs home filesystem.
2. Cut the directory in Strata.
3. Paste it into a destination on another filesystem, such as `/tmp` mounted as tmpfs.
4. Observe the operation failure.

### Expected behavior
Strata should move the directory across filesystems by recursively copying it safely to the destination and deleting the source only after the copy succeeds. Cancellation or failure should leave the source intact and remove incomplete destination staging data.

### Screenshots or video
A screenshot captured during manual testing shows the error dialog text: `Can't recursively copy directory`.

No relevant terminal output; the operation failed through the handled UI error path.

### Additional context
Reproduced reliably while testing cancellation of an eight-directory move from `/home` (Btrfs) to `/tmp` (tmpfs). All source directories remained and the destination stayed empty. Same-filesystem directory moves use rename semantics and do not expose this failure.

issues.body:
### Problem or use case

Strata cannot preview some extensionless dotfiles that contain plain text, such as `.steampath` or `.steamid`. Similar dotfiles whose MIME type is already recognized, such as `.bash_profile`, can be previewed, so the behavior is inconsistent.

A typical reproduction is:

1. Select a non-executable, extensionless dotfile containing text (for example, `.steampath`).
2. Press Space to preview it.
3. Strata reports that no preview is available instead of showing the file contents.

### Proposed solution

Treat extensionless dotfiles as bounded plain text when none of their execute bits are set and no more specific preview provider recognizes them. Keep existing MIME/type-specific handling, and do not apply this fallback to executable dotfiles.

### Alternatives considered

An allowlist for names such as `.steampath` and `.steamid` would fix individual cases but would not cover arbitrary application dotfiles. Relying only on MIME detection produces the current inconsistency.

### Visual examples

N/A — this changes preview eligibility rather than the preview UI.

### Strata version

Not provided; reported against the current preview behavior.

### Additional context

Plain-text reads should retain the existing size limit and safety behavior.

## Description

On SMB/GVfs mounts (and other locations that don't support Trash), the only delete action available was "Move to Trash", which fails with "This location doesn't support Trash. Delete permanently instead." The resulting "Completed with errors" dialog only had a "Done" button — no way to actually delete the item short of dismissing the error, re-selecting the item, and manually choosing the separate "Permanently delete" context-menu action.

This tracks which failed entries were specifically trash-unsupported failures (as opposed to some other, unrelated error) through `OperationEvent::CompletedWithErrors` and `BrowserEvent::OperationCompletedWithErrors`, as a list of retryable locations. When that list is non-empty, the completion dialog now also offers a "Delete Permanently" button; choosing it reuses the existing permanent-delete confirmation dialog, scoped to just the entries that actually failed for that reason — not ones that already succeeded, or failed for some unrelated reason (e.g. a permission error).

## Visual evidence

Screenshots attached below showing the full flow against a real trash-unsupported mount:
1. The "Completed with errors" dialog now offers "Delete Permanently" alongside "Done", instead of being a dead end.
2. Clicking it chains into the existing permanent-delete confirmation dialog, scoped to just the retryable item.
3. Confirming actually deletes the file — Strata shows "This directory is empty" and the filesystem agrees.

## How to test

1. Find or create a location GIO refuses to trash into — e.g. `/tmp` itself reliably reproduces this (`gio trash <file-in-tmp>` fails with "Trashing on system internal mounts is not supported"), or use a real SMB/GVfs mount as in the original report.
2. In Strata, select a file there and press Delete (or trigger a batch delete).
3. Observe the "Completed with errors" dialog now includes a "Delete Permanently" button.
4. Click it, confirm the follow-up "Permanently delete N?" dialog.

**Expected result:** the item is actually deleted, with no dead-end error state.

I verified this exact flow end to end (not just via unit tests) against `/tmp` as the trash-unsupported destination.

## Related issue

Closes #179

issues.body:
**Strata version:** 0.7.0 (GitHub release archive, x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu; source commit `f2594d106d8fdb878b786b445c61379d391e2c0f`)

**Installation method:** GitHub release archive

**Linux distribution and desktop environment:** Omarchy (Arch-derived), Hyprland on Wayland, glibc 2.44, GTK 4.22

## What happened?

On an SMB share mounted through GVfs (`smb://…`, backend `gvfsd-smb`), the file context menu offers only **Move to Trash** (Delete). Because GVfs SMB mounts do not implement GIO's Trash protocol, deleting fails with **"This location doesn't support Trash. Delete permanently instead."** There is no **Delete permanently** entry in the context menu, so files on SMB mounts cannot be deleted from the UI at all. A batch delete additionally produces a "Completed with errors" dialog whose only button is **Done** — there is no actionable way to complete the permanent deletion.

Worth noting: the release binary *does* contain a **Permanently delete** context-menu action (bound to Delete, marked `danger`) and calls `g_file_delete_async` for permanent deletion — but it is not surfaced on trash-less mounts.

## Steps to reproduce

1. In Strata, press **Ctrl+L**, enter `smb://<server>/<share>`, press Enter to open an SMB mount.
2. Right-click a file or folder on the share.
3. Observe the context menu lists only **Move to Trash** (Delete) — there is no **Delete permanently** option.
4. Press Delete (or trigger a batch delete).
5. The error appears: "This location doesn't support Trash. Delete permanently instead." (batch: "Completed with errors … Delete permanently instead." with only a **Done** button).
6. The item remains; there is no way to delete it from Strata.

## Expected behavior

Strata should offer a **Delete permanently** option (with a destructive-action confirmation) on filesystems that don't support Trash — for example, swap *Move to Trash* → *Delete permanently* via `g_file_delete_async` on such mounts, or include it as a distinct context-menu item. The "this location doesn't support Trash" dialog should also provide an actionable **Delete permanently** confirmation instead of only **Done**.

## Screenshots

- Context menu on an SMB mount showing only *Move to Trash* (no permanent-delete option).
- "Completed with errors" dialog: *1 item could not be deleted … This location doesn't support Trash. Delete permanently instead.* with only a *Done* button.

## Relevant logs

```text
WARN strata::ui::browser: unable to open file backend=native error_domain=g-io-error-quark error_code=15
```

## Additional context

- Reproducible on any GVfs SMB mount (tested against a Samba/Ubuntu server). Other non-local GVfs mounts that lack Trash are presumably affected too.
- Local filesystem trashing works fine — only remote/trash-less mounts are affected.
- Workaround (not ideal): delete from a terminal on the gvfs mount path, e.g. `rm -r "/run/user/1000/gvfs/smb-share:server=…,share=…/folder"`.
- The README's feature list includes a "permanent delete" file operation, so this appears to be a gap between the shipped capability and what's surfaced on trash-less mounts.

## What changed and why

Fixes #229. Two keyboard-first issues:

1. **`y`/`p` shortcuts** — the right-click context menu advertises `Y` (Copy path) and the Pin action, but no keyboard binding existed. Added `BrowserView::copy_path()` and `BrowserView::pin_focused()`, wired to `y`/`Y` and `p`/`P` in the window key handler.
2. **Copied paths not shell-safe** — Copy path returned a raw, unescaped path with no trailing slash. Added `copy_path_text()` / `shell_escape_path()` so native directory paths get metacharacters escaped (e.g. space → `\ `) and a trailing `/`. Native files keep the escaped path without the slash; URIs are unchanged.

## How to exercise

1. Navigate to a directory with a space, select a folder such as `Movies⁄TV`, and press `y`.
2. Paste into a shell — expect `/mnt/Mass\ 1/Movies⁄TV/`.
3. Focus a folder and press `p` — expect it to pin to the sidebar.

## Expected result

- `y`/`Y` copies the focused/selected path; `p`/`P` pins the focused folder.
- Copied native directory paths are escaped with a trailing slash.

## Checklist / notes

- `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`, and `cargo test --all-targets --all-features` all pass (445 tests, including 3 new regression tests).

## Description

Use Unicode case folding when comparing display names so uppercase and lowercase entries are interleaved conventionally. Names that fold to the same value use their original spelling as a deterministic tie-breaker, and secondary name ordering uses the same comparison.

## Visual evidence

N/A — this changes item ordering only and does not alter the interface layout or styling.

## How to test

1. Create a folder containing `apple`, `Banana`, `cherry`, and `Date`.

issues.body:
## Summary

Sorting by name appears to use raw byte/code-point ordering, so all uppercase names sort before all lowercase ones (`A-Z`, then `a-z`). Every mainstream file manager instead sorts case-insensitively, interleaving the two (`Aa-Zz`).

## Steps to reproduce

1. Create a folder containing `apple`, `Banana`, `cherry`, `Date`.
2. Open it in Strata and sort by Name ascending.

## Actual

```
Banana
Date
apple
cherry
```

## Expected

```
apple
Banana
cherry
Date
```

## Why

Case-insensitive name sorting is the convention in GNOME Files, Dolphin, Windows Explorer, and macOS Finder. Byte-order sorting scatters related names apart purely by capitalisation, which reads as a bug rather than a deliberate ordering.

## Notes

- Ties (names differing only by case) should still fall back to a deterministic comparison so ordering is stable.
- Related, if not already handled: natural ordering for embedded numbers, so `file2` sorts before `file10`.
- This is about collation order only, not about the sort-preference persistence covered by #40 / #44.

body: ## Description Completes SFTP support on Strata’s URI-native GIO/GVfs path. After integrating current `main`, SFTP receives scheme-appropriate credential fields, actionable connection errors, sanitized backend messages and logs, and a disposable OpenSSH fixture. At the owner’s request after live testing, **SFTP host-key questions now use a Strata-styled dialog** instead of GTK’s native question window. It preserves every backend choice and index, never trusts automatically, and warns when GVfs supplies no fingerprint (`???`); verify the key out of band before continuing. Cancel, Escape, and close silently return to the previous folder. Other schemes and device mounts retain GTK’s native question handling. Password prompts remain scheme-specific; a backend key-passphrase request is labelled “Passphrase,” but the local GVfs/OpenSSH probe did not emit one for an encrypted key. Remote validation, listing, and diagnostic failures now share the mount-error sanitizer so URI user-info, query, and fragment do not leak through those paths. The fixture and [SFTP guide](docs/remote-sftp.md) clarify that OpenSSH can skip host-key checks for loopback and that encrypted keys may be unlocked by `ssh-add` before Strata connects. ## Visual evidence **Before — GTK’s native trust question:** **After — Strata-styled trust question:** Pending owner upload of the sanitized live-GVfs capture through GitHub’s PR editor; do not treat the local capture as an attached image. The original author’s [SFTP sign-in image](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/spandan11106/strata/pr-assets/sftp-auth-dialog.png) remains separate evidence for its password-field changes. ## How to test 1. Start `./scripts/sftp-fixture.sh --port 2222`, add its client key to a disposable SSH agent, then open its printed `sftp://` address with Ctrl+L. The fixture should browse without a password prompt; enter a folder, use Back/Forward, and open a remote file. 2. For host-key testing, use a **locally restricted non-loopback relay** and an isolated `known_hosts`: loopback may skip trust checks. Reject the first question with Cancel or Escape and verify no error or password dialog follows. Reconnect only after independently verifying the server fingerprint; rotate the fixture’s host key to exercise the changed-key path, without accepting an unverified replacement. 3. Use a password-enabled test account to enter a wrong password, retry, cancel, then authenticate successfully. Use an unused port for refused-connection guidance and `sftp://bad.invalid/` for hostname guidance. The [manual matrix](docs/remote-sftp.md) lists the remaining conditional backend cases. **Expected result:** trusted authentication browses the requested folder; choices are never answered automatically; rejected trust and cancelled sign-in leave the previous location; incorrect credentials retry with only relevant fields; genuine failures give actionable guidance without exposing URI secrets. ## Related issue Closes #63

issues.body:
## Summary

Complete and verify first-class SFTP support on top of the URI-native GIO/GVfs foundation merged in #31. Strata currently accepts `sftp://` and uses a protocol-agnostic mount flow, but only SMB has been exercised end to end and the custom `gio::MountOperation` explicitly handles only password prompts.

## Scope

- Support and test:
  - password-based SFTP;
  - SSH-key authentication;
  - encrypted-key passphrases;
  - optional usernames and non-default ports;
  - unknown and changed host-key confirmation.
- Handle the applicable `GMountOperation` question/choice signals rather than silently accepting or dropping backend trust decisions.
- Preserve the existing user-driven credential retry flow without automatic prompt loops.
- Preserve the prior committed location and history when authentication is cancelled or rejected.
- Add actionable runtime guidance when the SFTP GVfs backend is unavailable without treating one distribution package name as universal.
- Map common failures such as host not found, connection refused, timeout, permission denied, authentication failure, and host-key rejection to recoverable UI.
- Verify URI-native navigation, breadcrumbs, history, Miller descent, hover peek, clipboard/drag export, and opening files through the default application.
- Add a disposable OpenSSH SFTP fixture for integration/manual coverage.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `sftp://host/path` and `sftp://user@host:2222/path` browse successfully when reachable.
- [ ] Password and SSH-key authentication both work.
- [ ] Encrypted keys can request a passphrase through the backend flow.
- [ ] Unknown or changed host keys require an explicit user decision and are never silently trusted.
- [ ] Wrong credentials can be corrected without flicker or retry loops.
- [ ] Cancelling authentication restores the previous location without adding history.
- [ ] Missing backend and common network/authentication failures produce actionable, sanitized messages.
- [ ] No password, passphrase, key material, username, host, or remote path leaks into normal-level logs.
- [ ] Module tests cover mount prompt/question state transitions and cancellation.
- [ ] Disposable OpenSSH integration coverage exercises authentication, browsing, cancellation, failure, and host-key decisions.
- [ ] New controls and states follow Strata theming, accessibility, and Lucide icon requirements.

## Context

Follow-up to #20 and #31. SMB is the only remote protocol currently verified end to end.

author: spandan11106
body:
## Description

Adds an optional **Group by file type** view setting for Explorer and Grid modes. When it is on,
directories go into a **Folder** group and files sit under labels from the shared MIME database
("JSON document", "Markdown document", "Python script", …), so they read the way they do elsewhere
on the desktop. Folders lead, the remaining groups are alphabetical, and the pane's own sort order
is preserved inside each group. The Miller-column mode is untouched, and the setting is stored with
the other view preferences.

Explorer grouping uses list-view sections, so it keeps one selection, keyboard navigation, and
marquee drags. Grid views have no section headings, so a grouped grid renders one heading and grid
per type: a pane can now hold several sections, selection is reported to the browser as the union
across them, one marquee drag runs through all of them, and a plain click clears the groups it did
not land in.

Two consequences worth flagging for a grouped grid: arrow-key movement and shift-click stay inside
the group they start in, and each group pins its column count to what the pane width allows,
because a grid only knows its row count once its columns are fixed.

Six commits, each self-contained and green on its own: the section and marquee refactors land
first with no behaviour change, then the setting, then Explorer grouping, then Grid grouping.

## Visual evidence

**Explorer**

![Explorer grouped by file type](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/spandan11106/strata/feat/192-group-by-file-type/docs/screenshots/type-grouping-explorer.png)

**Grid**

![Grid grouped by file type](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/spandan11106/strata/feat/192-group-by-file-type/docs/screenshots/type-grouping-grid.png)

## How to test

1. Create a directory with several file types, e.g. `mkdir -p demo/{Projects,Notes}` and
   `touch demo/{config.json,package.json,README.md,notes.md,plain.txt,script.py,style.css}`.
2. Open it in Strata and switch to Explorer mode from the appearance menu.
3. Enable **Group by file type** in the same menu.
4. Switch to Grid mode; scroll, then select items with click, ctrl+click, and a marquee drag across
   two groups.
5. Sort by another column, type in the pane filter, and toggle hidden files.
6. Turn the setting off again, and switch to the list (Miller-column) mode.

**Expected result:** Explorer and Grid divide entries into labeled type sections with folders
first; sorting inside a group follows the column header or sort menu; filtering and hidden-file
toggles drop a group once it is empty; selection survives across groups; the setting is remembered
across restarts; and the ungrouped views and the Miller-column mode look and behave exactly as
before.

## Related issue

Closes #192

issues.body:
### Problem or use case

Directories with many different kinds of files are harder to scan when every item appears in one continuous list. Grouping items into labeled sections by file type would make related files easier to find at a glance.

### Proposed solution

Add an optional **Group by file type** view setting for Explorer and Grid modes.

When enabled:
- Place directories in a **Folder** group.
- Group files under user-facing type labels such as **JSON document**, **Markdown document**, **Plain text document**, or **Python script**.
- Preserve the selected sort order within each group.
- Show a clear heading for each group; Grid mode should use the same grouping with grid items beneath each heading.
- Keep the spatial Miller-column mode unchanged.

### Alternatives considered

Sorting by type puts similar files next to one another, but it does not provide labeled visual sections and makes boundaries between types less obvious.

### Visual examples

Follow the familiar file-manager pattern where the view is divided by type headings—for example, **Folder**, **JSON document**, **Markdown document**, **Plain text document**, and **Python script**—with matching items listed or tiled below each heading.

### Strata version


### Additional context

This should be scoped to Explorer and Grid modes only, not the Miller-column mode.

body:
## Description

Build and update only the active browser mode instead of constructing hidden Columns, Grid, and Explorer views during every navigation. Rebuild the selected view from the browser snapshot when switching modes so navigation state and loaded entries are preserved.

This removes synchronous hidden-widget construction from directory navigation, including empty directories, and avoids duplicate model updates in inactive modes.

## Visual evidence

N/A — this is a non-visual navigation performance change.

## How to test

1. Open Strata in Columns mode and navigate repeatedly through populated and empty directories.
2. Switch between Columns, Grid, and Explorer after a directory has loaded, then continue navigating in each mode.
3. Confirm each mode immediately shows the current directory, entries, selection, loading state, and empty-directory state.

**Expected result:** Navigation constructs and updates only the visible browser mode, while switching modes preserves the complete current directory view.

## Related issue

Closes #113

issues.body:
### Strata version

0.6.1 (source build at commit `e00117a79f1ab3d9ee2150a53b87a94300397d8c`).

### Installation method

Built from source.

### Linux distribution and desktop environment

Omarchy 4.0.2 (Arch Linux), Hyprland 0.56.2, Wayland.

### What happened?

Strata constructs hidden Grid and Explorer pane widgets whenever a directory column is added, even when Columns is active. In Grid or Explorer mode it also inserts every entry into both the visible mode model and the hidden Columns model. This adds unnecessary GTK widget construction plus a second O(n) set of string allocations and model splices.

On a deterministic 100,000-entry fixture, three optimized runs per mode produced these medians:

| Mode | Enumeration | Peak PSS | Difference from Columns |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Columns | 1,884 ms | 216,818 KiB | baseline |
| Grid | 2,714 ms | 254,386 KiB | +44.1% time, +17.3% PSS |
| Explorer | 2,081 ms | 235,571 KiB | +10.5% time, +8.6% PSS |

The whole-mode deltas include each view's own rendering cost, but the duplicate hidden-model splice is independently visible in the event path and scales with every entry.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run `./scripts/generate-fixture.sh target/fixtures` and `cargo build --release`.
2. Close other Strata processes and create isolated settings for each browser mode:

   ```shell
   for mode in columns grid explorer; do
     mkdir -p "/tmp/strata-$mode/strata"
     printf 'mode = "theme"\ntheme = "azure-glow"\nbrowser_mode = "%s"\n' "$mode" \
       > "/tmp/strata-$mode/strata/settings.toml"
   done
   ```

3. Run each mode three times in its own D-Bus session, substituting `columns`, `grid`, and `explorer` for `MODE`:

   ```shell
   MODE=columns
   dbus-run-session -- env \
     XDG_CONFIG_HOME="/tmp/strata-$MODE" \
     STRATA_BINARY=target/release/strata \
     ./scripts/profile-fixture.sh target/fixtures/100000
   ```

4. Record complete-enumeration time and peak PSS, then compare the three modes.

### Expected behavior

Only the active browser mode should construct panes and receive incremental entry insertions. Switching modes should build/rebuild the newly active view from the existing browser snapshot, as the mode-switch paths already support.

### Screenshots or video

N/A — no recording was captured; benchmark output is included below.

### Relevant logs

```shell
Columns: PSS 216818,218468,213839 KiB; enumeration 1994,1875,1884 ms
Grid:    PSS 254386,254657,254162 KiB; enumeration 2714,2691,2792 ms
Explorer:PSS 235608,235075,235571 KiB; enumeration 2398,2061,2081 ms
```

### Additional context

- Benchmark environment: AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D, 32 GiB RAM, Linux 7.1.9-arch1-2, GTK 4.22.4, optimized release build, warm filesystem cache.
- `src/ui/browser.rs:3053` forwards every event to `ModeViews`.
- `src/ui/browser_modes.rs:497-530` constructs both a Grid pane and an Explorer pane for every `ColumnAdded`, regardless of `self.mode`.
- `src/ui/browser_modes.rs:488-496` similarly rebuilds both alternate views on truncation.
- `src/ui/browser_modes.rs:532-543` inserts batches into the active Grid/Explorer model.
- `src/ui/browser.rs:3066-3085` then inserts the same batch into the Columns model without checking the active mode.
- `EntriesReplaced` already has the missing Columns-mode guard at `src/ui/browser.rs:3089-3100`.
- `ModeViews::set_mode` already rebuilds the selected alternate mode (`src/ui/browser_modes.rs:419-435`), and `BrowserView::set_view_mode` already calls `sync_column_models` when returning to Columns (`src/ui/browser.rs:541-546`, `3374-3395`).
- The alternate modes were introduced by `06ad2af3` (`Add grid and explorer browser modes`).
- Open PR #83 adds up to four independently navigable panes, each with its own `BrowserView`, but leaves the hidden-view construction and duplicate model-update paths intact. It changes both `src/ui/browser.rs` and `src/ui/browser_modes.rs`, so the recommended sequence is to merge/rebase #83 first, then implement this optimization on top and refresh the source-line references and benchmarks. The multi-pane flow can amplify the current cost, but that impact has not yet been measured.
- Open issue #59 targets preview dependencies and hidden Settings construction on the startup path; it does not cover hidden browser views or duplicate per-directory model updates.

#### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Navigation constructs only the active mode's pane widgets.
- [ ] Grid and Explorer loads do not mutate hidden Columns models.
- [ ] Switching back to Columns still shows the complete, sorted directory.
- [ ] The 100,000-entry benchmark shows lower Grid/Explorer PSS and enumeration time without regressing Columns.
- [ ] After PR #83, the benchmark covers both one-pane and four-pane layouts and confirms that work scales only with visible views.

Strata can already toggle hidden files from **Appearance → Hidden files**, and `Ctrl + H` is implemented, but the feature is difficult to discover. ### Alternatives considered

Keep the option only in the Appearance menu and document `Ctrl + H`. This does not address in-product discovery. Replacing `Ctrl + H` outright could disrupt existing users, so adding `Ctrl + .` as an alias is preferred.

N/A — this is a discoverability and keyboard interaction improvement to the existing hidden-files control.

Current development build (`9a9381f`).

The existing toggle is implemented in the top-bar Appearance popover. `Ctrl + H` is handled by the window key controller but is currently absent from the Keyboard Shortcuts page.

body: ## Description Two parts, both from #155: **Menu typography audit.** The per-item right-click menu (`.item-context-menu`) already scales its text to `0.88em`, but three sibling popovers never got the same treatment and rendered at the unscaled root size: the Sort By popover (`.column-menu`, also reused by the Settings video-backend dropdown), the top-bar Appearance popover (`.appearance-menu`), and the folder-background context menu (`.folder-context-menu`, also reused for the Trash/Network/pinned-place sidebar menus). Brought all three to the same `0.88em` already established by `.item-context-menu`, rather than inventing a new value. **App-wide text size.** Added a Text size control (Small/Medium/Large) under Theme & appearance. It's backed by a new persisted `text_size` preference, and applies by setting the root `window` font-size through `ThemeManager`'s existing higher-priority CSS provider (the same mechanism that already injects `@define-color` theme tokens on every theme change). Since virtually everything in `style.css` is sized in `em` relative to that root, one root font-size change scales the whole app proportionally — no per-widget overrides needed, and existing size hierarchy (headings vs. labels vs. secondary text) is preserved. Applies live, no restart required. ## Visual evidence New Text size control: ![typography settings](attach in PR comment) Home directory at each size (Small / Medium / Large), verified via a fully isolated dev build (separate D-Bus session, so it couldn't touch the running installed app) with each size persisted to config and the app relaunched fresh — confirms the setting is read correctly at startup, not just applied live: Screenshots attached in a follow-up comment. ## How to test 1. Open Settings → Theme & appearance. A new TYPOGRAPHY section appears between the System card and the theme grid, with a Text size row (Small/Medium/Large), Medium selected by default. 2. Switch between the three — the whole app's text (sidebar, file list, breadcrumbs, settings itself) should resize immediately, no restart needed. 3. Quit and relaunch Strata — the chosen size should still be in effect. 4. Open the top-bar Appearance menu (list icon) and the Sort By menu (column header) — their text should now read at the same smaller, denser size as the per-item right-click menu (right-click a file), instead of looking larger than the rest of the UI. 5. Right-click empty folder space, and right-click Trash/Network/a pinned place in the sidebar — those context menus should also read at the smaller size now. **Expected result:** text size setting persists and applies live app-wide; the four affected menus (Sort By, Appearance, folder-background context menu, sidebar context menus) all read at the same size as the already-correct per-item context menu. ## Related issue Closes #155

author: pdwaldrop
body: ## Description #8 covers collision checks, traversal, deletion, and transfer all being separate path-based GIO calls — between any two of them, another process in a shared writable directory can swap a path component and redirect the operation, and recursion trusted the `FileEntry` type recorded when an item was originally listed rather than re-checking it. This covers the **permanent-delete** half specifically, called out in the issue as the most important case. For local paths, deletion now walks descriptor-relative to each already-open directory file descriptor instead of re-resolving path strings: - Opens each directory once via `openat2` with `RESOLVE_BENEATH | RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS | RESOLVE_NO_MAGICLINKS` (the exact flags the issue names), relative to the parent's fd — never by re-walking a path from `/`. - Re-reads each entry's real type with `statat(..., SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW)` immediately before deciding whether to recurse or unlink, instead of trusting the `FileEntry.kind` the item was listed with. A directory that's since become a symlink is deleted as the symlink it now is, not opened as a directory. - If a component changes after that check but before the corresponding open (the one window that's fundamentally irreducible), the `RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS` open fails closed with a clear error rather than following it. - Mirrors the `openat`/`O_NOFOLLOW` walk the archive extractor (`ExtractionDestination`) already uses for the same reason, rather than introducing a second technique. - Remote (GVfs) locations have no local descriptor to walk against, so they keep the existing path-based `permanently_delete` — explicit, not silently claiming an equivalent guarantee. - Mid-delete cancellation responsiveness is preserved: each child recurses through its own async hop (checking `Cancellable::is_cancelled()` before each), matching the granularity the old GIO-async version had. The existing `cancelling_recursive_delete_leaves_the_unfinished_root_in_place` test (unchanged) continues to pass against the new backend and was run 8x back-to-back to rule out timing flakiness. **Out of scope for this PR:** copy and move still walk GIO paths and have the same class of exposure. Extending this same descriptor-relative approach to them is a natural, separately-reviewable follow-up — the issue's acceptance criteria mention "copy/delete" together, so I'm leaving #8 open rather than closing it here. ## Visual evidence Nothing in the UI changes, but here's a live reproduction of the fix itself: a folder (`target`) containing a real subdirectory plus a symlink (`decoy-link`) pointing outside the tree to a sentinel file, permanently deleted via Shift+Delete in Strata. 1. `target` selected, containing the decoy symlink. 2. The permanent-delete confirmation. 3. `target` is gone after confirming. 4. The symlink's target folder, opened afterward — `sentinel.txt` untouched, same size and timestamp as before. The same scenario is also covered deterministically by the two new adversarial unit tests (top-level and nested). ## How to test 1. Create a folder containing a real subdirectory with a file, plus a symlink pointing somewhere outside that folder (e.g. `ln -s /somewhere/else decoy`). 2. Select the folder in Strata and permanently delete it (Shift+Delete, or the "Permanently delete" context-menu item). 3. Confirm the folder and the symlink itself are gone, and whatever the symlink pointed to is untouched. 4. `cargo test` — two new tests (`permanent_delete_removes_a_symlink_standing_in_for_a_directory_without_following_it`, `permanent_delete_does_not_follow_a_symlink_nested_inside_the_tree`) cover this at both the top level and nested inside a recursive delete. **Expected result:** a symlink anywhere in a deleted tree — whether it was always there or swapped in for a real directory — is removed as itself, never followed to whatever it points to. ## Related issue Related to #8 (permanent-delete portion; copy/transfer hardening left as follow-up)
title: fix(operations): harden local permanent delete against symlink races

author: pdwaldrop
body:
## Description

Follow-up to #253 (permanent-delete hardening), covering the other half of #8: copying. `copy_recursively` is the single function behind paste-copy, the cross-filesystem move fallback, and staged replace's copy-to-stage step — walking its source the same path-based way delete used to (enumerate, then re-resolve each child's own path next call), trusting whatever type GIO reported at listing time.

For fully local source/target pairs, `copy_recursively` now dispatches to a descriptor-relative walk, mirroring #253's approach:

- Each source directory is opened once via `openat2` with `RESOLVE_BENEATH | RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS | RESOLVE_NO_MAGICLINKS`, and every entry's real type is re-read immediately before deciding what to do with it — never trusted from an earlier listing.
- Symlinks are recreated directly (`readlinkat` + `symlink`), never followed.
- Regular files still go through GIO's own `copy_async` unchanged, except for one thing: instead of the original (re-resolvable) path, it's handed a `/proc/self/fd/<n>` reference to the fd already opened and verified via `openat2`, kept alive for the call's duration. That keeps GIO's metadata handling, progress reporting, and any reflink optimization completely untouched, while pinning what actually gets read to the exact object already checked — immune to the name being swapped afterward.
- The **destination** side stays on GIO throughout and needed no change: every call site here already writes to a private, freshly created staging name first and only becomes visible via the existing atomic `renameat2` commit, so it isn't exposed to the same class of race.
- Remote (GVfs) locations keep the existing path-based copy — explicit, not claiming an equivalent guarantee.
- Move's primary path is already a single atomic rename and needed no change; only its cross-filesystem fallback (when rename returns `WouldRecurse`) goes through this same hardened `copy_recursively`.

**One non-obvious wrinkle worth flagging for review:** `/proc/self/fd` entries are themselves reported as symlinks by `lstat`, so `NOFOLLOW_SYMLINKS` has to be dropped from the GIO copy call for the regular-file case specifically. Keeping it caused GIO to copy the magic-link's *target path text* as a new symlink instead of the file's actual bytes — caught immediately by the existing `moving_a_directory_falls_back_to_a_safe_copy_when_the_move_would_recurse` test, which started failing until this was found and fixed. Left a comment on that line explaining why.

## Visual evidence

N/A — this changes how local copies read the source tree internally; nothing in the UI changes. Two rounds of manual verification instead of screenshots (folder-listing screenshots of a copy operation don't show anything a picture can capture — the interesting part is on disk):

1. **Metadata preservation**: copied a folder where one file had unusual permissions (`754`) through the real app (Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V). The copy landed with `-rwxr-xr--` — exact match — confirming the `/proc/self/fd` handoff didn't regress GIO's metadata copying.
2. **Symlink safety**: copied a folder containing a symlink pointing outside the tree to a sentinel file, through the real app. Destination:
   ```
   to/source/nested/decoy -> .../outside-sentinel   (a real symlink, not a directory)
   ```
   `outside-sentinel/secret.txt` was never touched or duplicated into the destination.

New adversarial unit tests cover the same two scenarios (nested symlink, top-level symlink) deterministically.

## How to test

1. Create a folder containing a real subdirectory with a file, plus a symlink pointing somewhere outside that folder.
2. Copy it in Strata (Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V, or drag to another pane) into a new location.
3. Confirm the copy succeeds, the symlink is recreated as a symlink (not expanded into a real directory), and whatever it points to is untouched.
4. `cargo test` — `copy_recursively_does_not_follow_a_symlink_nested_inside_the_tree` and `copy_recursively_of_a_symlink_creates_a_symlink_not_a_recursive_copy`.

**Expected result:** a symlink anywhere in a copied tree is recreated as a symlink pointing at the same target, never followed into a real copy of its contents.

## Related issue

Related to #8 (copy half; delete covered by #253)
title: fix(operations): harden local copy against symlink races

author: pdwaldrop
body:
## Description

**Depends on #253** (not yet merged) — built directly on that branch since this needs `permanently_delete_local_path` from it. GitHub is showing #253's commits as part of this diff for now; once #253 merges into `main`, this PR's diff will automatically narrow to just the commits below. The actual new content of this PR is the last commit only.

Four internal cleanup deletes still called the old GIO-based `permanently_delete`, each deciding directory-vs-file from a type determined once, well before the (potentially slow) operation it was cleaning up after:

- `replace_local_with`, after the atomic exchange: deleting whatever the old target turns out to be, using `target_is_directory` computed before the copy-to-stage step.
- `replace_local_with`, `move_source` cleanup: deleting the original source after a successful replace-as-move, using `source_is_directory` from the same early check.
- `move_local_with`'s `WouldRecurse` fallback: deleting the source after a cross-filesystem copy finishes.
- `copy_new_recursively`'s cancellation cleanup.

All five `permanently_delete` call sites (these four, plus the user-facing delete request handler from #253) now go through a new shared `permanently_delete_maybe_local` helper — local paths get the descriptor-relative walk, which re-reads each entry's real type itself and never accepts a caller-supplied hint at all; remote (GVfs) locations keep the existing GIO delete. This also de-duplicates the local-vs-remote dispatch that was written inline in #253's delete handler.

**Worth being direct about what this does and doesn't demonstrate**, since I want to flag this for review rather than let the commit message undersell or oversell it: GIO's `NOFOLLOW_SYMLINKS` already made a symlink standing in for a tracked directory at these specific call sites fail safe — I added a test for exactly that (`replacing_a_directory_cleans_up_a_symlink_in_the_old_contents_without_following_it`) and confirmed by temporarily reverting one call site that it **passes against the pre-existing code too**. So this isn't closing a bug that test demonstrates.

What it actually buys is protection the old path-based approach structurally cannot offer, and that a static symlink-substitution test can't exercise: once a directory is opened as a descriptor, nothing that happens to its *name* afterward — unlink-and-recreate, rename, anything short of touching the open file itself — can redirect an already-open fd to something else. That's a property of what a file descriptor is, not something provable by a single-shot unit test. This change closes that gap at every internal cleanup site instead of only the one path a user's delete click reaches directly, and stops trusting a type hint (`target_is_directory`/`source_is_directory`) that may be stale by the time it's acted on — matching the issue's "avoid trusting stale type metadata for recursion decisions" criterion, even though these aren't literally `FileEntry` values.

## Visual evidence

N/A — internal cleanup path, no UI change. Manually verified the replace-with-conflict flow still works correctly end-to-end in the app: pasted a folder onto an existing same-named folder, chose Replace, confirmed the new content landed and the old content was fully cleaned up (`old-item.txt` gone, `item.txt` has the new content).

## How to test

1. `cargo test` — the new `replacing_a_directory_cleans_up_a_symlink_in_the_old_contents_without_following_it`, plus the existing `staged_directory_replacement_does_not_merge_old_contents` / `staged_file_replacement_*` tests, which continue to pass unchanged against the new dispatch.
2. In the app: paste a folder onto an existing same-named folder and choose Replace. Confirm the new content lands and old content is fully gone.

**Expected result:** no behavior change visible to the user; internal cleanup after replace/move now shares the same race-safe, type-revalidating delete as the user-facing one.

## Related issue

Related to #8 (closes the remaining "stale type" gap across delete/copy/replace cleanup paths)
title: fix(operations): stop trusting stale types for replace/move cleanup

v8.0.0

v8 - What's new

[!IMPORTANT] actions/download-artifact@v8 has been migrated to an ESM module. This should be transparent to the caller but forks might need to make significant changes.

[!IMPORTANT] Hash mismatches will now error by default. Users can override this behavior with a setting change (see below).

Direct downloads

To support direct uploads in actions/upload-artifact, the action will no longer attempt to unzip all downloaded files. Instead, the action checks the Content-Type header ahead of unzipping and skips non-zipped files. Callers wishing to download a zipped file as-is can also set the new skip-decompress parameter to true.

Enforced checks (breaking)

A previous release introduced digest checks on the download. If a download hash didn't match the expected hash from the server, the action would log a warning. Callers can now configure the behavior on mismatch with the digest-mismatch parameter. To be secure by default, we are now defaulting the behavior to error which will fail the workflow run.

ESM

To support new versions of the @actions/* packages, we've upgraded the package to ESM.

Bumps [actions/github-script](https://github.com/actions/github-script) from 8.0.0 to 9.0.0.
Release notes

Sourced from actions/github-script's releases.

v9.0.0

New features:

  • getOctokit factory function — Available directly in the script context. Create additional authenticated Octokit clients with different tokens for multi-token workflows, GitHub App tokens, and cross-org access. See Creating additional clients with getOctokit for details and examples.
  • Orchestration ID in user-agent — The ACTIONS_ORCHESTRATION_ID environment variable is automatically appended to the user-agent string for request tracing.

Breaking changes:

  • require('@actions/github') no longer works in scripts. The upgrade to @actions/github v9 (ESM-only) means require('@actions/github') will fail at runtime. If you previously used patterns like const { getOctokit } = require('@actions/github') to create secondary clients, use the new injected getOctokit function instead — it's available directly in the script context with no imports needed.
  • getOctokit is now an injected function parameter. Scripts that declare const getOctokit = ... or let getOctokit = ... will get a SyntaxError because JavaScript does not allow const/let redeclaration of function parameters. Use the injected getOctokit directly, or use var getOctokit = ... if you need to redeclare it.
  • If your script accesses other @actions/github internals beyond the standard github/octokit client, you may need to update those references for v9 compatibility.
